period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 8 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: What Does Per Cent Really Mean?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 1.1 p.1
textbook_items_in_class.description: Surya mixes red and yellow paint; red makes up 3/4 of the mixture. Convert 3/4 to a percentage using equivalent fractions and two algebraic methods. Answer: 75%.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 1.1 p.2
textbook_items_in_class.description: Surya saves 2/5 of prize money for a canvas. Express 2/5 as a percentage using three methods (equivalent fraction, cross-multiplication, bar model). Answer: 40%.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Express 24% as a fraction. Since percentage = fraction over 100, 24% = 24/100 = 12/50 = 6/25. Generalises: z% equals any fraction equivalent to z/100.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Nandini has 25 marbles, 15 white. What percentage are white? Choose from given options (MCQ).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.1 p.3

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: what does the word 'percentage' literally mean? Invite students to guess, then reveal the Latin origin — 'per centum', meaning 'out of hundred'. Draw a 100-square grid on the board and shade portions to anchor the idea that every percentage is a fraction with denominator 100.

Walk through Example 1, section 1.1 p.1 ("Surya mixes red and yellow paint; red makes up 3/4....") using equivalent-fraction scaling (×25 numerator and denominator to reach /100) and the cross-multiplication method side by side on the board. Ask students to confirm that both routes reach 75%.

Work through Example 2, section 1.1 p.2 ("Surya saves 2/5 of prize money for a canvas....") together, then immediately reverse the direction with Example 3, section 1.1 p.3 ("Express 24% as a fraction...."), so students see the fraction→percentage and percentage→fraction conversions as two faces of one idea.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3 ("Nandini has 25 marbles, 15 white....") individually, writing their working before checking the MCQ options. Cold-call two students to explain which method they used; draw out that multiple routes (equivalent fraction, cross-multiplication) all agree.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the direction of conversion — whether to multiply or divide by 100 — so reinforce that 'per cent' already means '/100', making the fraction form immediate. Watch for errors when the denominator does not divide 100 evenly (e.g., 1/3), where cross-multiplication must be used rather than equivalent-fraction scaling. Example 2, section 1.1 p.2 provides a self-study worked example of the bar-model method that can be suggested for students who want a visual anchor.
materials: Squared or grid paper for 100-square model

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: 15 of 80 students come to school by walking. What percentage come by walking?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.1 p.3
textbook_items_in_class.description: Match four runners (A, B, C, D) shown at different positions on a race track to their approximate percentage completion from a given set (55%, 20%, 38%, 72%, 84%, 93%).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.1 p.4
textbook_items_in_class.description: Insert >, <, or = without calculating: (i) 50% __ 5%; (ii) 5/10 __ 50%; (iii) 3/11 __ 61%; (iv) 30% __ 1/3.

time_bands.activity: Begin with the motivating comparison from section 1.1: which biscuit has more sugar — one where 9 out of 34 g is sugar, or one where 13 out of 45 g is? Students discuss in pairs for a brief spell, then share intuitions. Establish that converting both fractions to percentages (using the fraction-to-percentage method built on in the earlier unit) resolves the ambiguity cleanly.

Students solve Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3 ("15 of 80 students come to school by walking....") and Figure it Out Q4, section 1.1 p.3 ("Match four runners … to their approximate percentage completion....") in pairs, choosing their own conversion method. Circulate; prompt pairs whose fractions don't divide 100 evenly to use cross-multiplication.

Class attempts Figure it Out Q5, section 1.1 p.4 ("Insert >, <, or = without calculating: 50% __ 5%; 5/10 __ 50%; 3/11 __ 61%; 30% __ 1/3....") independently, using reasoning rather than computation. Reveal answers on the board, then have students verify item (iii) and (iv) by calculating — showing that estimation and calculation agree.

Brief class discussion: why does base 100 make comparisons easier than comparing raw fractions? Students write one sentence in their notebooks summarising the advantage of percentages for comparison, drawing on the biscuit example and the FDP trio (fraction, decimal, percentage) that the section introduces.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is assuming that 3/11 < 61% without checking — students may guess that small-denominator fractions are small; press them to convert before concluding. The FDP trio (fractions, decimals, percentages are interchangeable) is the conceptual anchor of section 1.1 and should be named explicitly when students debate Q5. For self-study, Example 3, section 1.1 p.3 provides additional practice converting a percentage back to a simplified fraction.

periods.activity_title: Finding the Part: y% of a Quantity

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 1.2 p.5
textbook_items_in_class.description: Madhu eats 120 g of 25%-sugar biscuits (30 g sugar); Madhav eats 95 g of 35%-sugar biscuits (33.25 g sugar). Multiple methods: ratio, proportional equation, unit-rate. Concludes Madhav consumed more sugar.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 1.2 p.8
textbook_items_in_class.description: Zubin needs 80% of 75 marks to get an A grade. Three methods: fraction multiplication (4/5 × 75 = 60), decimal multiplication (0.8 × 75 = 60), proportional reasoning with bar model. Answer: 60 marks.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.12
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing numbers using percentage bar models: (i) 20% of ? = 12 (given 100% shown); (ii) ? is 60% of 75; (iii) ? is 140% of ?, with two unknowns and bar models provided.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.12
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the value and draw bar models for: (i) 25% of 160; (ii) 16% of 250; (iii) 62% of 360; (iv) 140% of 40; (v) 1% of 1 hour; (vi) 7% of 10 kg.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.2 p.12
homework.description: Surya made 60 ml of deep orange paint with red paint making up 3/4. How much red paint was used? (Apply percentage/fraction to find a quantity.)

time_bands.activity: Return to the biscuit comparison from section 1.1: now the question shifts from which biscuit has a higher sugar percentage to how many grams of sugar are actually consumed. Pose the question from Example 1, section 1.2 p.5 ("Madhu eats 120 g of 25%-sugar biscuits; Madhav eats 95 g of 35%-sugar biscuits....") and invite students to guess who consumed more sugar before any calculation.

Work through Example 1, section 1.2 p.5 using the ratio method and the proportional equation method on the board. Then work Example 3, section 1.2 p.8 ("Zubin needs 80% of 75 marks....") showing fraction multiplication (4/5 × 75) and decimal multiplication (0.8 × 75) side by side, so students see that y% of a value means (y/100) × value regardless of method.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.12 ("Find missing numbers using percentage bar models: 20% of ? = 12; ? is 60% of 75; ? is 140% of ?....") in pairs, drawing bar models in their notebooks. Emphasise reading the bar model as a proportional strip before writing any equation.

Class begins Figure it Out Q2, section 1.2 p.12 ("Find the value and draw bar models for: 25% of 160; 16% of 250; 62% of 360; 140% of 40; 1% of 1 hour; 7% of 10 kg...."), completing as many parts as time allows. Students choose their own method (fraction, decimal, or bar) and record alongside each answer which method they used.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently apply the percentage to the wrong quantity — in the biscuit example, multiplying 25% by 35 rather than by 120; reinforce that the percentage always acts on the quantity it belongs to. The bar model in Figure it Out Q1, section 1.2 p.12 is the most powerful diagnostic: a student who can draw the strip correctly almost always sets up the equation correctly. For a further worked example of unit-rate method, Example 1, section 1.2 p.5 can be revisited independently.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 1.2 p.7
textbook_items_in_class.description: Free-hand computation table: find 25%, 10%, 20%, 5% of values 100, 200, 50, 80, 10, 35, 287 without pen and paper, exploiting the relationships between percentages (e.g., 20% = 2 × 10%).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: How Close Can You Get?, p.8
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students work in pairs, each choosing a number; both independently estimate the percentage equivalent of the fraction a/b (a < b) formed by the two numbers and announce answers within 5 seconds. The closer estimate wins. Played for 10 rounds to build proportional number sense.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 6, section 1.2 p.10
textbook_items_in_class.description: Kishanlal's daily sales vs. ₹5000 target: Day 1 ₹2000 = 40%, Day 2 ₹3500 = 70%, Day 3 ₹5000 = 100%, Day 4 ₹6000 = 120%. Introduces percentages greater than 100. Students compute Days 5–8.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Insert >, <, = without computing (verify after estimating): (i) 50% of 510 vs. 50% of 515; (ii) 37% of 148 vs. 73% of 148; (iii) 29% of 43 vs. 92% of 110; (iv) 30% of 40 vs. 40% of 50; (v) 45% of 200 vs. 10% of 490; (vi) 30% of 80 vs. 24% of 64.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 1.2 p.13
homework.description: Fill in the blanks: (i) 3 is __% of 300; (ii) __ is 40% of 4; (iii) 40 is 80% of __.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the free-hand computation table from Example 2, section 1.2 p.7 ("Free-hand computation table: find 25%, 10%, 20%, 5% of values 100, 200, 50, 80, 10, 35, 287...."). Students fill in selected cells without pen and paper, then the class discusses the doubling/halving relationships — 20% is double 10%, 5% is half of 10% — that make mental calculation fast.

Run Activity: How Close Can You Get?, p.8 ("Students work in pairs … estimate the percentage equivalent of a/b … announce within 5 seconds … closer estimate wins....") for several rounds. Each student picks a number, the pair forms a fraction, both estimate silently, then announce. Debrief after several rounds: which fractions were easy to estimate and why?

Introduce percentages greater than 100 using Example 6, section 1.2 p.10 ("Kishanlal's daily sales vs. ₹5000 target: Day 1 ₹2000 = 40%... Day 4 ₹6000 = 120%...."). Students compute Days 5–8 individually. Discuss: what does 120% mean physically — it is 20% above the target, so the whole exceeds the reference.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q4, section 1.2 p.13 ("Insert >, <, = without computing: 50% of 510 vs. 50% of 515; 37% vs. 73% of 148; 29% of 43 vs. 92% of 110...."), reasoning about each comparison without arithmetic first, then verifying one or two to confirm.

periods.teacher_notes: Errors around percentages exceeding 100 are common — students may say '120% is impossible'. Use Kishanlal's sales table from Example 6, section 1.2 p.10 to make the concrete case that the reference (target of ₹5000) and the measured value (₹6000) are different quantities. In the estimation activity, students who double-count the denominator as part of the fraction need a quick redirect to the definition of a/b where a < b. Example 7, section 1.2 p.12 (farmer harvest at 250%) extends the beyond-100% idea further and makes a good self-study pointer.
materials: No additional materials needed for mental-calculation phase

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 1.2 p.9
textbook_items_in_class.description: Millet kanji: millet-to-water ratio is 2:7, so millet is 2/9 of mixture. Estimate first, then compute 2/9 × 100 = 22.22%. For 500 ml of mixture, millet = 5 × 22.22 = 111.1 ml.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 5, section 1.2 p.10
textbook_items_in_class.description: A cyclist has covered 40% (92 km) of the Delhi-to-Agra route. Find remaining distance using four methods: proportional equation (d = 230, remainder = 138 km), ratio method, percentage scaling (40% → 20% → 60%), and algebraic setup.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.2 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks using scaling relationships: (i) given 30% of k = 70, find 60%, 90%, 120% of k; (ii) given 100% of m = 215, find 10%, 1%, 6%; (iii) given 90% of n = 270, find 9%, 18%, 100%; (iv) make 2 more questions for peers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 1.2 p.13
textbook_items_in_class.description: Workers pick coffee berries in 20% of a plantation in 18 days. How long to cover the whole plantation at the same rate? Why must we assume constant rate?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 1.2 p.13
homework.description: Badminton training: warm-up:play:cool-down = 10%:80%:10% of 90 minutes. Find the duration of each activity.

time_bands.activity: Work through Example 4, section 1.2 p.9 ("Millet kanji: millet-to-water ratio is 2:7....") showing how a ratio becomes a fraction of the whole (millet is 2 out of 9 parts total), then converting to a percentage and using it to find the millet volume in 500 ml. Students write an estimate before the calculation and compare.

Demonstrate the reverse problem using Example 5, section 1.2 p.10 ("A cyclist has covered 40% — 92 km — of the Delhi-to-Agra route...."), showing at least two of the four methods (proportional equation and percentage scaling). Pose the question: given a part and its percentage, find the whole — a skill that underpins many later applications.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q5, section 1.2 p.13 ("Fill in the blanks using scaling relationships: 30% of k = 70, find 60%, 90%, 120% of k....") in small groups, using doubling and tripling relationships rather than repeated full calculations. Groups also attempt one peer-question (part iv) and exchange with another group.

Class works Figure it Out Q9, section 1.2 p.13 ("Workers pick coffee berries in 20% of a plantation in 18 days....") together: find total time, then discuss why the 'constant rate' assumption is essential. Students articulate the assumption in their own words before the teacher confirms.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often find reverse-percentage problems (given a part and its percentage, find the whole) harder than forward problems; anchor this in the bar model — the full bar is the unknown, the shaded portion and its label are both given. The ratio-to-fraction step in Example 4, section 1.2 p.9 is a common stumbling point: students may treat millet as 2/7 (forgetting that the total parts are 2 + 7 = 9). Example 9, section 1.2 p.10 provides additional multi-method practice for self-study.

periods.activity_title: Comparing Scores, Price Changes, and Profit or Loss

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 1.3 p.14
textbook_items_in_class.description: Eesha: English score 42/50 = 84%, Science score 70/80 = 87.5%. Resolves apparent ambiguity about which is better by converting both to percentages. Science score is higher.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 1.3 p.17
textbook_items_in_class.description: Kishanlal buys a sweater at ₹300, marks it at ₹480, sells at ₹430. Profit = ₹130 on CP of ₹300 → percentage profit = 130/300 × 100 = 43.3%. Students also find wholesaler and manufacturer profit percentages.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 5, section 1.3 p.17
textbook_items_in_class.description: Raghu buys rice at ₹35/kg, sells 10 kg for ₹300 (CP = ₹350). Loss = ₹50. Percentage loss = 50/350 × 100 = 14.28%.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shopkeeper buys a geometry box for ₹75 and sells for ₹110. Find profit margin with respect to cost.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.19
textbook_items_in_class.description: Petrol price was ₹60 in 2015 and ₹100 in 2025. Find percentage increase. Choose from MCQ options.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.3 p.19
homework.description: Carpenter's cost for a chair is ₹475 with a desired 50% profit margin. Find the selling price.

time_bands.activity: Introduce section 1.3's first application: using percentages to compare scores on different scales. Work through Example 1, section 1.3 p.14 ("Eesha: English score 42/50 = 84%, Science score 70/80 = 87.5%....") — students see that without conversion, comparing 42/50 and 70/80 is opaque, but a percentage makes the comparison immediate.

Introduce percentage increase and decrease through the tomato price and theatre footfall examples from section 1.3, then develop profit and loss terminology: cost price, marked price, selling price, profit margin, loss percentage. Work through Example 4, section 1.3 p.17 ("Kishanlal buys a sweater at ₹300... percentage profit = 130/300 × 100 = 43.3%....") on the board.

Work Example 5, section 1.3 p.17 ("Raghu buys rice at ₹35/kg, sells 10 kg for ₹300....") to establish percentage loss, stressing that the percentage is always computed on the cost price. Students individually compute the loss amount and percentage, then check against the example.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.19 ("Shopkeeper buys a geometry box for ₹75 and sells for ₹110....") and Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.19 ("Petrol price was ₹60 in 2015 and ₹100 in 2025....") in pairs. Cold-call one pair for each and discuss whether the percentage is always calculated on the original (base) value.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent misconception is computing profit percentage on the selling price rather than the cost price; reinforce the definition: percentage profit = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100. Example 6, section 1.3 p.17 (Shyamala's vase with 18% loss) provides a useful self-study item where students can practise the two-method approach (deducting loss amount vs. multiplying by 82%). Students should also note that percentage increase/decrease always uses the original value as the base.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 7, section 1.3 p.21
textbook_items_in_class.description: ₹6000 deposited at 10% p.a. for 3 years. Option 1 (no compounding): interest returned each year, total = ₹7800. Option 2 (compounding): interest added back each year, total = ₹7986. Side-by-side tables build intuition.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 9, section 1.3 p.23
textbook_items_in_class.description: Generalises to principal p, rate r, time t. Without compounding: total = p(1 + rt). With compounding: total = p(1 + r)^t. Derivation shown step by step for both options.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 10, section 1.3 p.24
textbook_items_in_class.description: TV bought at ₹21,000; depreciates 5% after 1 year. Two equivalent methods: reduce by 5% (21000 − 1050 = ₹19,950) or multiply by 95% (0.95 × 21000 = ₹19,950).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.22
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bank of Yahapur: 10% p.a. Compare the return on ₹20,000 for 2 years with and without annual compounding.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 1.3 p.24
textbook_items_in_class.description: A city's population rises 3% every year. Current population is 1.5 crore. Find expected population after 3 years.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.23
homework.description: Post office: 7% p.a. Find interest on ₹50,000 for 3 years without compounding. How much more with compounding?

time_bands.activity: Build intuition for compounding by working Example 7, section 1.3 p.21 ("₹6000 at 10% p.a. for 3 years: Option 1 no compounding → ₹7800; Option 2 compounding → ₹7986....") iteratively in a side-by-side table on the board. Students fill in one column (no compounding) independently, then the class builds the compounding column together, discovering that Year 2's principal is Year 1's total.

Generalise the pattern to Example 9, section 1.3 p.23 ("Without compounding: total = p(1 + rt); with compounding: total = p(1 + r)^t...."). Show the step-by-step derivation for compounding, linking each year's multiplier (1 + r) to the iterative table above. Students identify what changes between the two formulas.

Introduce depreciation as negative compounding with Example 10, section 1.3 p.24 ("TV bought at ₹21,000; depreciates 5% after 1 year: 0.95 × 21000 = ₹19,950...."). Show both methods (subtract loss amount vs. multiply by 0.95) and ask students which generalises to multi-year depreciation more easily — leading them to the multiplicative form.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 1.3 p.22 ("Bank of Yahapur: 10% p.a., ₹20,000 for 2 years, compare with and without compounding....") and begin Figure it Out Q8, section 1.3 p.24 ("City population rises 3% every year, current 1.5 crore, find after 3 years...."), applying the p(1+r)^t formula. Class discusses how population growth mirrors the compounding structure.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often apply the simple-interest formula (p × r × t) when compounding is intended, or vice versa; the side-by-side table in Example 7, section 1.3 p.21 is the clearest way to make the structural difference visible before introducing symbols. For depreciation, emphasise that multiplying by (1 − r) each period is exactly the same logic as compounding, just with r subtracted rather than added. Example 11, section 1.3 p.24 (village population over three decades) extends depreciation to multi-period contexts and is a useful self-study pointer.

periods.activity_title: Tricky Percentages: Sequential Discounts, Margins, and Surprises

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 12, section 1.3 p.26
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cakely offers 30% + 20% sequential discount vs. Cakify's flat 50%. On ₹200 cake: Cakely → ₹140 → ₹112 (44% total reduction); Cakify → ₹100 (50% reduction). Compounding of discounts means 30% + 20% < 50%.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 13, section 1.3 p.27
textbook_items_in_class.description: Surbhi marks goods at 50% profit margin (1.5x), then offers 50% discount (0.75x). Results in 25% loss, not break-even. Derives the correct discount for break-even: 33.33%. Bar model illustrates the three price levels.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.28
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shopkeeper sets price with 35% profit margin, then offers 30% discount on selling price. Does he make a profit or a loss? Give reasons.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 1.3 p.28
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore: 5% of 40 = 40% of 5; 25% of 12 = 12% of 25; 15% of 60 = 60% of 15. Generalise: is x% of y always equal to y% of x? Justify algebraically.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 1.3 p.29
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bus fares increased 3% last year and 4% this year. Find overall percentage price increase over 2 years.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q14, section 1.3 p.30
homework.description: Try This: 100 people, 99% left-handed. How many left-handed people must leave to bring the percentage down to 98%?

time_bands.activity: Open with a deliberate misconception: 'A shop offers 30% off and then 20% off. Is that the same as 50% off?' Let students vote, then work through Example 12, section 1.3 p.26 ("Cakely: 30% + 20% sequential discount vs. Cakify's flat 50%: on ₹200 cake, Cakely gives ₹112, Cakify gives ₹100....") step by step. Students identify at which step the arithmetic diverges from the naive addition.

Work through Example 13, section 1.3 p.27 ("Surbhi marks goods at 50% profit margin, then offers 50% discount — results in 25% loss....") using the bar model showing three price levels (cost price, marked price, selling price). Students derive algebraically why 1.5x × 0.5 = 0.75x and find the correct discount rate for break-even (33.33%) as a deductive consequence of the formula.

Students work Figure it Out Q5, section 1.3 p.28 ("Shopkeeper sets price with 35% profit margin, then offers 30% discount on selling price....") and Figure it Out Q10, section 1.3 p.29 ("Bus fares increased 3% last year and 4% this year; find overall percentage increase....") in pairs. The bus-fare problem connects sequential increases to the compounding structure established in the interest unit.

Class investigates Figure it Out Q7, section 1.3 p.28 ("Explore: 5% of 40 = 40% of 5; 25% of 12 = 12% of 25; generalise: is x% of y always equal to y% of x?...."). Students write the algebraic justification (x/100 × y = y/100 × x) and discuss one surprising consequence: computing a difficult percentage (e.g., 37% of 200) by swapping to 200% of 37 is always valid.

periods.teacher_notes: The central deductive insight of this unit is that sequential percentage changes multiply their scale factors rather than add their percentages: a 30% followed by a 20% discount gives 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 of the original, not 0.5. Students who see this structure will not fall into the additive trap in Figure it Out Q10, section 1.3 p.29 or in novel compound-discount problems. Watch for students who compute the second discount on the original price rather than the reduced one — the bar model from Example 13, section 1.3 p.27 corrects this visually.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly states the meaning of 'per cent'?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Out of every hundred. The word 'per cent' comes from the Latin 'per centum', meaning 'out of hundred', so a percentage is always a fraction with denominator 100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition: percentage = fraction with denominator 100, derived from 'per centum'.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing percentage with the prefix 'deci-' or with fractions out of ten.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be confusing percentage with the prefix 'milli-' or with fractions per thousand.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has no specific misconception pattern — likely a random guess or confusion with half of 100.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the word origin (per centum) in section 1.1 before answering.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give one more example of a Latin-origin word in everyday life that means 'hundred'.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 1.1 p.3
exercise.description: Nandini has 25 marbles, 15 white. What percentage are white? Choose from given options (MCQ).

assessment_items.note: no goals routed to this section in the chapter

items.prompt: In a class of 60 students, 18 travel to school by bicycle. What percentage of the class travels by bicycle? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 30%. The fraction of students who cycle is 18/60. Converting to a percentage: (18/60) × 100 = 1800/60 = 30.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the part as a fraction of the whole and multiply by 100 using the fraction-to-percentage method from section 1.1.

inclusivity.support: Draw a bar divided into 60 equal parts, shade 18, and use the bar to read off the percentage visually.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the class size to 72 students with the same 18 cyclists and re-solve — note how the percentage changes and explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 1.1 p.3
exercise.description: 15 of 80 students come to school by walking. What percentage come by walking?

items.prompt: A recipe requires that 20% of the total mixture is sugar. If the total mixture weighs 250 g, how many grams of sugar are needed? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 50 g. Using the principle that y% of a value equals (y/100) × value: (20/100) × 250 = 0.2 × 250 = 50 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the formula: percentage of a quantity = (y/100) × quantity, as established in section 1.2.

inclusivity.support: Draw a percentage bar showing the full 250 g as 100% and mark 20% on it before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: If sugar is increased to 25% of the same total mixture, by how many grams does the sugar quantity change — and what fraction of the original sugar amount is that increase?

exercise.description: Find missing numbers using percentage bar models: (i) 20% of ? = 12 (given 100% shown); (ii) ? is 60% of 75; (iii) ? is 140% of ?, with two unknowns and bar models provided.

items.prompt: Without calculating exactly, which of the following is definitely greater?

options.label: D
options.text: Cannot be determined without a calculator

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare by computing (y/100) × value for each expression, or reason that 30% of 500 = 30 × 5 while 60% of 200 = 60 × 2, so 150 > 120.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student likely reasoned that 60% > 30% without considering that the base quantities differ, applying only the percentage without the base.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have cancelled 60/200 against 30/500 incorrectly, or guessed without reasoning.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not recognise that mental estimation is sufficient — a strategy developed in section 1.2's free-hand and comparison exercises.

inclusivity.support: Write each expression as a fraction of its base and use the 10%-doubling strategy from Example 2, section 1.2 p.7 to estimate each mentally.
inclusivity.challenge: Change 30% of 500 to 30% of 400 and determine without full computation which side wins — justify with a scaling argument.

items.prompt: A runner has completed 45% of a race and has already covered 54 km. What is the total length of the race, and how many kilometres remain? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total length = 120 km; remaining = 66 km. If 45% corresponds to 54 km, then 1% = 54/45 = 1.2 km, so 100% = 120 km. Remaining = 100% − 45% = 55% = 55 × 1.2 = 66 km. Alternatively, set up 45/100 = 54/d to get d = 120 and remainder = 120 − 54 = 66 km.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the reverse-percentage method: find 1% = known amount ÷ given percentage, then scale to 100% and the remaining percentage.

inclusivity.support: Draw a bar labelled 100% for the full race distance, mark 45% of it, and use the bar to set up the proportional equation.
inclusivity.challenge: If the runner maintains pace and covers 10% more of the race every hour, how many hours does the remaining 55% take?

items.prompt: A shopkeeper purchases a bag of rice for ₹480 and sells it for ₹528. Find the percentage profit on the cost price. Show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply: percentage profit = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100, as defined in section 1.3.

inclusivity.support: Draw a bar showing ₹480 as 100% (cost price) and ₹48 profit as the additional segment, then read off the percentage from the proportional strip.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the selling price that would give the shopkeeper a 25% profit on the same cost price of ₹480.

items.prompt: ₹10,000 is deposited in a bank at 8% per year for 2 years. Find the total amount at the end of 2 years (a) without compounding (simple interest added but not reinvested) and (b) with annual compounding. Show your working for both.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Without compounding: total = p(1 + rt) = 10000 × (1 + 0.08 × 2) = 10000 × 1.16 = ₹11,600. (b) With annual compounding: total = p(1 + r)^t = 10000 × 1.08² = 10000 × 1.1664 = ₹11,664.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two formulas from section 1.3: without compounding p(1+rt); with compounding p(1+r)^t.

inclusivity.support: Build a year-by-year table like the one in Example 7, section 1.3 p.21, filling in the amount at the end of each year for both options before writing the formula.
inclusivity.challenge: By how many rupees does compounding outperform simple interest after 3 years at the same rate? Explain in one sentence why the gap grows with more years.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper marks a jacket at 40% above cost price and then offers a 20% discount on the marked price. Does the shopkeeper make a profit or a loss on the cost price, and by what percentage? Show your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The shopkeeper makes a 12% profit. Let cost price = 100. Marked price = 140 (40% above cost). Selling price after 20% discount = 140 × 0.8 = 112. Profit = 112 − 100 = 12. Percentage profit on cost price = 12%.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the scale factors: (1 + 0.4) × (1 − 0.2) = 1.4 × 0.8 = 1.12, so the selling price is 112% of cost price, giving a 12% profit.

inclusivity.support: Use a concrete cost price (₹100) and draw three price levels on a bar: cost price, marked price, selling price — compute each step numerically.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the exact discount percentage the shopkeeper would need to offer on the marked price to break even (sell at exactly cost price).
